results.title: Order and totient sum do not determine simplicity (Kourovka 19.25)
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: There are finite groups $G$ and $H$ of the same order with $\sum_{g \in G} \varphi(|g|) = \sum_{h \in H} \varphi(|h|)$, where $|g|$ is the order of $g$ and $\varphi$ is Euler's totient function, such that $G$ is simple and $H$ is not simple. So the Curtin–Pourgholi question has a negative answer.

results.title: Expectation under a probability mass function
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type carrying a σ-algebra in which singletons are measurable, let $p$ be a probability mass function on $\alpha$ and let $f : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$. The expectation of $f$ under $p$ is the Bochner integral $\int f \, d\mu_p$, where $\mu_p$ is the probability measure on $\alpha$ associated to $p$.

results.title: Expectation as a series
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $p$ be a probability mass function on a measurable space $\alpha$ in which singletons are measurable, and let $f : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable with respect to the probability measure associated to $p$. Then the expectation of $f$ under $p$ equals the unordered sum $\sum_{a \in \alpha} p(a) f(a)$.

results.title: Expectation on a finite type
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $p$ be a probability mass function on a finite measurable space $\alpha$ in which singletons are measurable, and let $f : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$. Then the expectation of $f$ under $p$ equals the finite sum $\sum_{a \in \alpha} p(a) f(a)$.

results.title: Expectation of a constant on a finite type
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a finite set with a $\sigma$-algebra in which singletons are measurable and let $p$ be a probability mass function on $\alpha$. For every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, the expectation of the constant function $a \mapsto c$ under $p$ is $c$.

results.title: Expectation under the uniform distribution
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a nonempty finite type carrying a σ-algebra in which singletons are measurable. For every function $f : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$, the expectation of $f$ under the uniform distribution on $\alpha$ equals the average $\frac{1}{|\alpha|} \sum_{a \in \alpha} f(a)$.

results.title: Additivity of expectation on a finite type
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a finite set with a $\sigma$-algebra in which singletons are measurable, let $p$ be a probability mass function on $\alpha$, and write $\mathbb{E}_p[h]$ for the expectation of $h : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$ under $p$. For all $f, g : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$, $\mathbb{E}_p[f + g] = \mathbb{E}_p[f] + \mathbb{E}_p[g]$.

results.title: Homogeneity of expectation on a finite type
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a finite set with a $\sigma$-algebra in which singletons are measurable, let $p$ be a probability mass function on $\alpha$, and write $\mathbb{E}_p[h]$ for the expectation of $h : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$ under $p$. For every $c \in \mathbb{R}$ and $f : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$, the function $a \mapsto c\,f(a)$ has expectation $c\,\mathbb{E}_p[f]$.

results.title: Expectation of a scalar multiple
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $p$ be a probability mass function on a finite measurable space $\alpha$ in which singletons are measurable, let $c \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $f : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$. The expectation under $p$ of the scalar multiple $c f$ (the function $a \mapsto c \cdot f(a)$) equals $c$ times the expectation of $f$ under $p$.

results.title: Nonnegativity of expectation
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $p$ be a probability mass function on a finite measurable space $\alpha$ in which singletons are measurable, and let $f : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfy $f(a) \ge 0$ for every $a \in \alpha$. Then the expectation of $f$ under $p$ is nonnegative.

results.title: Monotonicity of expectation
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $p$ be a probability mass function on a finite measurable space $\alpha$ in which singletons are measurable, and let $f, g : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfy $f(a) \le g(a)$ for every $a \in \alpha$. Then the expectation of $f$ under $p$ is at most the expectation of $g$ under $p$.

results.title: Expectation of a finitely supported distribution
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $p$ be a probability mass function on a measurable space $\alpha$ in which singletons are measurable, and let $s$ be a finite subset of $\alpha$ such that $p(a) = 0$ for every $a \notin s$. Then for every function $f : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$, the expectation of $f$ under $p$ equals $\sum_{a \in s} p(a) f(a)$.

results.title: Expectation of an indicator
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $p$ be a probability mass function on a finite measurable space $\alpha$ in which singletons are measurable, and let $q$ be a property of elements of $\alpha$. results.title: Extended expectation
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a probability mass function $p$ on a type $\alpha$ and a function $f : \alpha \to [0, \infty]$, the extended expectation of $f$ under $p$ is the unordered sum $\sum_{a \in \alpha} p(a) f(a)$ in $[0, \infty]$, which always exists.

results.title: Extended expectation on a finite set
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $p$ be a probability mass function on a finite set $\alpha$. For every $f : \alpha \to [0, \infty]$, the extended expectation of $f$ under $p$ equals the finite sum $\sum_{a \in \alpha} p(a)\, f(a)$.

results.title: Extended expectation of a constant
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $p$ be a probability mass function on a set $\alpha$. For every $c \in [0, \infty]$, the extended expectation of the constant function $a \mapsto c$ under $p$ is $c$.

results.title: Extended expectation under the uniform distribution
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a nonempty finite type and $f : \alpha \to [0, \infty]$. The extended expectation of $f$ under the uniform distribution on $\alpha$ equals $|\alpha|^{-1} \sum_{a \in \alpha} f(a)$, computed in $[0, \infty]$.

results.title: Additivity of extended expectation
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $p$ be a probability mass function on a set $\alpha$, and write $\overline{\mathbb{E}}_p[h]$ for the extended expectation of $h : \alpha \to [0, \infty]$ under $p$. For all $f, g : \alpha \to [0, \infty]$, $\overline{\mathbb{E}}_p[f + g] = \overline{\mathbb{E}}_p[f] + \overline{\mathbb{E}}_p[g]$.

results.title: Extended expectation of a finite sum
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $p$ be a probability mass function on a set $\alpha$, and write $\overline{\mathbb{E}}_p[h]$ for the extended expectation of $h : \alpha \to [0, \infty]$ under $p$. For every index set $\iota$, finite subset $s \subseteq \iota$ and family of functions $f_i : \alpha \to [0, \infty]$ ($i \in \iota$), $\overline{\mathbb{E}}_p\bigl[a \mapsto \sum_{i \in s} f_i(a)\bigr] = \sum_{i \in s} \overline{\mathbb{E}}_p[f_i]$.

results.title: Extended expectation under a finitely supported distribution
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $p$ be a probability mass function on a set $\alpha$, and let $s \subseteq \alpha$ be a finite set with $p(a) = 0$ for every $a \notin s$. For every $f : \alpha \to [0, \infty]$, the extended expectation of $f$ under $p$ equals $\sum_{a \in s} p(a)\, f(a)$.

results.title: Change of variables for extended expectation
results.caption: Theorem

results.title: The parallelogram $P_{a,n}$
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For natural numbers $a$ and $n$, the set $P_{a,n} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ is the closed parallelogram spanned by $(1, 0)$ and $(a, n)$, that is, the set of points $s (1, 0) + t (a, n)$ with $0 \le s \le 1$ and $0 \le t \le 1$. For $n \ge 1$ it is the parallelogram with vertices $(0, 0)$, $(1, 0)$, $(a, n)$ and $(a + 1, n)$.

results.title: Integer affine maps of the plane
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a $2 \times 2$ integer matrix $M$ with entries $m_{ij}$ and an integer vector $u = (u_1, u_2) \in \mathbb{Z}^2$, the map $T_{M,u} : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ is $T_{M,u}(x, y) = (m_{11} x + m_{12} y + u_1, m_{21} x + m_{22} y + u_2)$, that is, $p \mapsto M p + u$. It is an affine unimodular map when $\det M = \pm 1$; the definition itself puts no condition on $\det M$.

results.title: Unimodularly equivalent sets
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Two sets $P, Q \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ are unimodularly equivalent when some affine unimodular map sends $P$ onto $Q$: there are a $2 \times 2$ integer matrix $M$ with $\det M = 1$ or $\det M = -1$ and an integer vector $u \in \mathbb{Z}^2$ such that $\{M x + u : x \in P\} = Q$.

results.title: Unimodular equivalence is reflexive
results.caption: Theorem

results.title: Clean lattice parallelogram

results.title: Clean parallelograms are unimodularly equivalent to standard ones

results.summary: Let $u$ and $v$ be lattice points spanning a clean lattice parallelogram $P$ whose area is an integer $n \ge 2$. Then there is an integer $a$ with $1 \le a < n$ and $\gcd(a, n) = 1$ such that $P$ is unimodularly equivalent to the standard clean parallelogram $P_{a,n}$.

results.title: Interior lattice points of a standard clean parallelogram
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $1 \le a < n$ with $\gcd(a, n) = 1$, let $P_{a,n} = \{s (1, 0) + t (a, n) : 0 \le s \le 1,\ 0 \le t \le 1\}$, and write $\langle x \rangle = x - \lfloor x \rfloor$ for the fractional part of a real number $x$. The lattice points in the interior of $P_{a,n}$ are exactly the points $\langle k(n - a)/n \rangle \, (1, 0) + (k/n) \, (a, n)$ for $k = 1, \dots, n - 1$.

results.title: The point reflection symmetry of $P_{a,n}$
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $a$ and $n$ be natural numbers with $1 \le a < n$ and $\gcd(a, n) = 1$, let $P_{a,n} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ be the parallelogram with vertices $(0, 0)$, $(1, 0)$, $(a, n)$, $(a + 1, n)$, and let $S : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ be $S(x, y) = (a + 1 - x, n - y)$. results.title: Number of steps of Euclid's algorithm
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For natural numbers $u$ and $v$, the number of division steps of Euclid's algorithm on $(u, v)$ is $0$ if $v = 0$, and otherwise one more than the number of division steps on $(v, u \bmod v)$.

results.title: Run of a sequential transducer
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The run of a sequential transducer $S$ from a state $q$ on an input word $a_1 \cdots a_n$ is the pair $(q_n, w_1 w_2 \cdots w_n)$, where $q_0 = q$ and, for each $1 \le i \le n$, $S$ moves from $q_{i-1}$ on $a_i$ to $q_i$ emitting the word $w_i$. The initial output and the final outputs of $S$ are not included.

results.title: Final state of a sequential transducer run
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a sequential transducer $S$, a state $q$ and an input word $w$, the final state of the run of $S$ from $q$ on $w$ is obtained by starting in $q$, reading the letters of $w$ in order, moving at each letter to the successor state given by the transition function of $S$, and taking the state reached at the end.

results.title: Output word of a sequential transducer run
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a sequential transducer $S$, a state $q$ and an input word $x$, the output word of the run from $q$ on $x$ is the concatenation of the output words that $S$ emits on the successive letters of $x$, starting in $q$ and moving to the successor state after each letter; the initial and final outputs are not included.

results.title: Final state of a sequential transducer run on a nonempty word
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $S$ be a sequential transducer, $q$ a state, $a$ an input letter and $w$ an input word, and let $q'$ be the successor state of $q$ on $a$ under the transition function of $S$. Then the final state of the run of $S$ from $q$ on the word $aw$ equals the final state of the run of $S$ from $q'$ on $w$.

results.title: Output of a sequential transducer on a nonempty word
results.caption: Theorem

The output word of the run of $S$ from $q$ on $ax$ is $w$ followed by the output word of the run from $q'$ on $x$.

results.title: Final state of a sequential transducer on a concatenation
results.caption: Theorem

results.title: Output of a sequential transducer on a concatenation
results.caption: Theorem

results.title: Translation by a sequential transducer

results.title: Mealy machine
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: A Mealy machine with state set $Q$, input alphabet $I$ and output alphabet $O$ consists of a start state in $Q$ and a transition function that, given a state $q \in Q$ and an input letter $a \in I$, returns a successor state in $Q$ and a single output letter in $O$; thus the output of a transition depends on the state and the input letter.

results.title: Run of a Mealy machine
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The run of a Mealy machine $M$ from a state $q$ on an input word $a_1 \cdots a_n$ is the pair $(q_n, o_1 \cdots o_n)$, where $q_0 = q$ and, for each $1 \le i \le n$, $M$ moves from $q_{i-1}$ on $a_i$ to $q_i$ emitting the output letter $o_i$.

results.title: Final state of a Mealy machine run
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a Mealy machine $M$, a state $q$ and an input word $x$, the final state of the run from $q$ on $x$ is the state reached by starting in $q$ and moving, on each successive letter of $x$, to the successor state given by the transition function of $M$; on the empty word it is $q$.

results.title: Mealy machine as a sequential transducer
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The sequential transducer of a Mealy machine $M$ has the states and the start state of $M$; on an input letter $a$ in a state $q$ it moves to the state that $M$ moves to and emits the one-letter word consisting of the letter that $M$ outputs on this transition. Every state accepts, and the initial and final outputs are empty.

results.title: The sequential transducer of a Mealy machine has the same final states
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a Mealy machine $M$, a state $q$ and an input word $w$, the final state of the run from $q$ on $w$ of the sequential transducer associated with $M$ equals the final state of the run of $M$ from $q$ on $w$.

results.title: The sequential transducer of a Mealy machine has the same run outputs
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a Mealy machine $M$, a state $q$ and an input word $w$, the output word of the run from $q$ on $w$ of the sequential transducer associated with $M$ (excluding its initial and final outputs) equals the output word of the run of $M$ from $q$ on $w$.

results.title: Every state of the sequential transducer of a Mealy machine is accepting
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a Mealy machine $M$, the set of accepting states of the sequential transducer associated with $M$ is the set of all states.

results.title: Initial output of the sequential transducer of a Mealy machine
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every Mealy machine $M$, the initial output of the sequential transducer of $M$ is the empty word.

results.title: Final outputs of the sequential transducer of a Mealy machine
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every Mealy machine $M$ and every state $q$, the final output of the sequential transducer of $M$ at $q$ is the empty word.

results.title: The sequential transducer of a Mealy machine computes its transduction
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every Mealy machine $M$, input word $x$ and output word $y$, the sequential transducer of $M$ translates $x$ to $y$ if and only if the transduction of $M$ on $x$ is $y$.

results.title: Moore machine
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: A Moore machine with state type $Q$, input alphabet $\Sigma$ and output alphabet $\Gamma$ consists of a transition function, assigning to each state $q$ and input letter $a$ a successor state $\delta(q, a) \in Q$, an output function $\lambda : Q \to \Gamma$, and a start state $q_0 \in Q$. The output depends only on the state.

results.title: Run of a Moore machine
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The run of a Moore machine $M$ with output function $\lambda$ from a state $q$ on an input word $a_1 \cdots a_n$ is the pair $(q_n, \lambda(q_0) \lambda(q_1) \cdots \lambda(q_n))$, where $q_0 = q$ and, for each $1 \le i \le n$, $q_i$ is the successor of $q_{i-1}$ on $a_i$. The output word has $n + 1$ letters and begins with the output of the starting state.

results.title: Final state of a Moore machine run
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a Moore machine $M$, a state $q$ and an input word $x$, the final state of the run from $q$ on $x$ is the state reached by starting in $q$ and moving, on each successive letter of $x$, to the successor state given by the transition function of $M$; on the empty word it is $q$.

results.title: Output word of a Moore machine run
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a Moore machine $M$, a state $q$ and an input word $x$, the output word of $M$ from $q$ on $x$ is the second component of the run of $M$ from $q$ on $x$: the outputs of the states visited along that run, starting with the output of $q$; it has one more letter than $x$.

results.title: Final state of a Moore machine run on a nonempty word
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a Moore machine $M$ with transition function $\delta$, a state $q$, an input letter $a$ and an input word $w$, the final state of the run of $M$ from $q$ on the word $aw$ equals the final state of the run of $M$ from $\delta(q, a)$ on $w$.

results.title: Output of a Moore machine on a nonempty word
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a Moore machine, $q$ a state, $a$ an input letter and $x$ an input word, and let $q'$ be the successor state of $M$ in state $q$ on letter $a$. The output word of the run of $M$ from $q$ on $ax$ is the output of $q$ followed by the output word of the run from $q'$ on $x$.

results.title: Transduction of a Moore machine
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $M$ be a Moore machine with start state $q_0$, and write $o(q)$ for the output of a state $q$. On an input word $a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n$, let $q_i$ be the state that $M$ moves to from $q_{i-1}$ on $a_i$. The transduction of $M$ on this word is the output word $o(q_0)\, o(q_1) \cdots o(q_n)$, of length $n + 1$.

results.title: The sequential transducer of a Moore machine
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $M$ be a Moore machine with transition function $\delta$, output function $\lambda$ and start state $q_0$. Its sequential transducer has the same states and the start state $q_0$; reading a letter $a$ in state $q$ it moves to $\delta(q, a)$ and emits the one-letter word $\lambda(\delta(q, a))$; every state is accepting; the initial output is the one-letter word $\lambda(q_0)$; and every final output is empty.

results.title: Moore machine output via its sequential rendering
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a Moore machine $M$, a state $q$ and an input word $x$, the output word of the run of $M$ from $q$ on $x$ is the output of $q$ followed by the output word of the run of the sequential rendering of $M$ from $q$ on $x$.

results.title: Every state of the sequential transducer of a Moore machine is accepting
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a Moore machine $M$, the set of accepting states of the sequential transducer associated with $M$ is the set of all states.

results.title: Initial output of the sequential transducer of a Moore machine
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every Moore machine $M$, the initial output of the sequential transducer of $M$ is the one-letter word consisting of the output of the start state of $M$.

results.title: Final outputs of the sequential transducer of a Moore machine
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a Moore machine $M$ and every state $q$, the final output word at $q$ of the sequential transducer associated with $M$ is empty.

results.title: The sequential transducer of a Moore machine computes its transduction
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every Moore machine $M$, input word $x$ and output word $y$, the sequential transducer of $M$ translates $x$ to $y$ if and only if the transduction of $M$ on $x$ is $y$.

results.title: Band check from a starting offset
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $w \in \mathbb{N}$ be a band width. For natural numbers $i$, $j$ and an alignment $A$, the band check of $A$ with width $w$ from offset $(i, j)$ is true exactly when every prefix $P$ of $A$ (including the empty prefix and $A$ itself) satisfies $|(i + p) - (j + q)| \le w$, where $p$ and $q$ are the numbers of columns of $P$ whose first, respectively second, entry is present.

results.title: Banded alignments
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $w \in \mathbb{N}$. An alignment $A$ is banded with width $w$ when, for every prefix of $A$ (including the empty prefix and $A$ itself), the number of columns of that prefix with a letter in the first row and the number with a letter in the second row differ by at most $w$.

results.title: Bound at an intermediate point, difference form
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For integers $a$, $d$, $t$ and $w$, if $|a| \le w$, $|a - d| \le w$ and $0 \le t \le d$, then $|a - t| \le w$.

results.title: Bound at an intermediate point, sum form
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For integers $a$, $d$, $t$ and $w$, if $|a| \le w$, $|a + d| \le w$ and $0 \le t \le d$, then $|a + t| \le w$.

results.title: A passing band check bounds the final offset
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $w, i, j \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $A$ be an alignment. If the band check of $A$ with width $w$ from offset $(i, j)$ is true, then $|(i + p) - (j + q)| \le w$, where $p$ and $q$ are the numbers of columns of $A$ whose first, respectively second, entry is present.

results.title: Banded alignments force close lengths
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $w \in \mathbb{N}$. If $A$ is a valid alignment of sequences $x$ and $y$ and $A$ is banded with width $w$, then the lengths of $x$ and $y$ differ by at most $w$, that is $\bigl| |x| - |y| \bigr| \le w$.

results.title: Diagonal alignment
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For sequences $x = x_1 \dots x_m$ and $y = y_1 \dots y_n$, let $k = \min(m, n)$. The diagonal alignment of $x$ and $y$ consists of the columns $(x_1, y_1), \dots, (x_k, y_k)$, which pair letters by position whether or not they are equal, followed by one column for each remaining letter of the longer sequence, in order, pairing that letter with a gap.

results.title: The diagonal alignment is a valid alignment
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For all sequences $x$ and $y$, the diagonal alignment of $x$ and $y$ is a valid alignment of $x$ and $y$: none of its columns consists of two gaps, and deleting the gaps from its first and second rows gives $x$ and $y$ respectively.

results.title: Columns using only the second sequence stay in the band
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $w, i, j \in \mathbb{N}$, let $y$ be a list of length $n$, and let $A$ be the alignment with one column for each element $b$ of $y$, in order, with empty first entry and second entry $b$. If $|i - j| \le w$ and $|i - (j + n)| \le w$, then the band check of $A$ with width $w$ from offset $(i, j)$ is true.

results.title: Columns using only the first sequence stay in the band
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $w, i, j \in \mathbb{N}$, let $x$ be a list of length $n$, and let $A$ be the alignment with one column for each element $a$ of $x$, in order, with first entry $a$ and empty second entry. If $|i - j| \le w$ and $|(i + n) - j| \le w$, then the band check of $A$ with width $w$ from offset $(i, j)$ is true.

results.title: The diagonal alignment stays in the band
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $w, i, j \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x$, $y$ be lists of lengths $m$ and $n$. If $|i - j| \le w$ and $|(i + m) - (j + n)| \le w$, then the band check of the diagonal alignment of $x$ and $y$ with width $w$ from offset $(i, j)$ is true.

results.title: The diagonal alignment is banded
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $w \in \mathbb{N}$. If two sequences $x$ and $y$ have lengths differing by at most $w$, that is $\bigl| |x| - |y| \bigr| \le w$, then the diagonal alignment of $x$ and $y$ is banded with width $w$.

results.title: The banded score is at most the Needleman–Wunsch score
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\sigma$ be an integer substitution score on an alphabet, $g$ an integer gap score and $w \in \mathbb{N}$ a band width. For sequences $x$ and $y$ over the alphabet and an integer $s$, if the banded score of $x$ and $y$ (under $\sigma$, $g$ and width $w$) is defined and equals $s$, then $s$ is at most the Needleman–Wunsch score of $x$ and $y$.

results.caption: Theorem

results.title: No banded score when the lengths differ by more than the band width
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\sigma$ be an integer substitution score on an alphabet, $g$ an integer gap score and $w \in \mathbb{N}$ a band width. For sequences $x$ and $y$ over the alphabet, of lengths $m$ and $n$, with $w < |m - n|$, the banded score of $x$ and $y$ (under $\sigma$, $g$ and width $w$) is undefined: no alignment of $x$ and $y$ is banded with width $w$.

results.title: The banded score is defined when the lengths are close
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Fix a substitution score $\sigma$, assigning an integer $\sigma(a, b)$ to each pair of letters $a$, $b$, an integer gap score $g$ and a band width $w \in \mathbb{N}$. If two sequences $x$ and $y$ have lengths differing by at most $w$, that is $\bigl| |x| - |y| \bigr| \le w$, then the banded alignment score of $x$ and $y$ (for $\sigma$, $g$ and $w$) is defined: it equals some integer $s$.

results.title: Number of gap columns of an alignment
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The number of gap columns of an alignment: columns with exactly one letter.

results.title: An alignment with few gap columns stays in the band from its start
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Along every prefix, the offset difference is at most the starting difference plus the number of gap columns: an alignment starting at `(i, j)` stays in the band of width `w` as soon as `|i - j| + gapColumns A ≤ w`.

results.title: An alignment with at most w gap columns is w-banded
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: An alignment with at most `w` gap columns is `w`-banded.

results.title: Alignment score is at most minus the number of gap columns
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: With nonpositive substitution scores and gap score at most `-1`, an alignment scores at most minus its number of gap columns.

results.title: The band lemma
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The band lemma (Ukkonen 1985): with nonpositive substitution scores and gap score at most `-1`, every alignment scoring at least `-w` (cost at most `w`) is `w`-banded.

results.title: The banded optimum is exact
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The banded optimum is exact when the optimal score is at least `-w` (optimal cost at most `w`), for nonpositive substitution scores and gap score at most `-1`: some optimal alignment exists and, by the band lemma, it is `w`-banded.
